newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say Israel wants calm over Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss say Israel wants calm over Holocaust funds.

text.p: Israel wants calm rather than confrontation over Swiss efforts to trace Jewish bank accounts lost in the Holocaust and assets from Nazi Germany, Swiss President Arnold Koller said on Friday.
Koller said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed in talks here that a calmer atmosphere was needed after weeks of rows between the Swiss and critics led by world Jewish groups.

"We agreed completely that we have every reason to cool down the public discussion. This emotional discussion is a threat and a danger to finding the real truth," Koller told reporters at the World Economic Forum in this Alpine resort.

Koller said he explained to Netanyahu the steps Berne and Swiss banks have taken to answer charges by major Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato that the Swiss profited cynically from World War Two.

The major steps were the creation of two commissions, one aiming to return to heirs bank accounts left by Holocaust victims and the other looking at Swiss financial ties with Hitler's Germany, including the flow of Nazi assets.
"We agreed that these investigations and the conclusions that we will draw from them must take place in an atmosphere of cooperation and not confrontation," Koller said.

The Swiss government has pledged to compensate victims of Nazi terror if the commisions turn up proof of Swiss wartime misdeeds. In the meantime, Swiss banks and businesses last week said they would set up a Holocuast memorial fund that Berne can join later.
"The Swiss banks have the same attitude. They wish to cooperate." Koller said.

Koller pledged that Berne rejected anti-Semitism after charges that racism was fuelled by remarks by former president and now Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz that Jewish demands for compensation were "blackmail".
"I also expressed to Netanyahu the deep regret felt by the Swiss government for the enormous and horrendous injustice of the Holocaust," Koller said.

The meeting with Netanyahu came one day after a top U.S. government official used nearly identical language on the Swiss hunt for assets, pledging to cooperate with the Swiss and urging an end to confrontational politics.

Commerce Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat said on Thursday after talks with Swiss banks and politicians that the Swiss investigations were a sincere effort. He rejected New York City Council threats to boycott Swiss banks.
"The statements by both Netanyahu and Eizenstat are moving in the same directions," Koller said.
